name: Retry / Backoff Resilience
description: solution_code (Python) defines a single top-level function retry_call(dependency, sleep) that wraps a harness-injected, harness-scripted flaky dependency callable and must retry it per the row's declared strategy_type/strategy_params, using ONLY the harness-injected sleep(seconds) callable for backoff delays -- never a real time.sleep(). The harness drives ONE call to retry_call() per row and checks three things: the exact sequence of delay values requested (bounds-checked, not exact-matched, for the one strategy_type whose delays are genuinely randomized), the exact number of real calls made to the dependency, and the final outcome (the dependency's own successful result value returned, or an exception propagated after every allowed attempt is exhausted). Ground truth is never trusted blindly: the harness FIRST independently recomputes, from strategy_type + strategy_params + dependency_behavior alone (via its own reference state-machine simulation of the declared strategy, never by inspecting solution_code or trusting the row's own claims), what the real call count/delay sequence/outcome must be, and rejects the row outright if the curator's own declared expected_result does not match that independent computation. Distinct from rate_limiting_policy_simulation (admission control under a fixed policy, never any retrying/waiting) and caching_strategy (storage/eviction, no failure/retry semantics at all): this category is specifically about resilience against a dependency that FAILS and must be retried, with correctly-computed backoff between attempts.
executionEnv: python3 (stdlib only). No real time.sleep()/time.time()/datetime.now() is EVER used to drive this category's timing -- every backoff delay is a plain number solution_code hands to the harness-injected sleep(seconds) callable, which records it and returns immediately without blocking, so a row whose backoff schedule spans simulated minutes still verifies in well under a second of real wall-clock time.

fields.label: Task description
fields.help: Natural-language description of the flaky dependency/scenario being retried, e.g. 'calling a payment gateway that intermittently times out' or 'fetching a config value from a service that is occasionally unavailable during deploys'. This is scenario framing/flavor text for the contributor and human/LLM audit stages -- the harness's own pass/fail decision is driven entirely by strategy_type + strategy_params + dependency_behavior + expected_result below, never parsed from this field.

fields.label: Retry strategy type
fields.help: Selects which of this harness's own independently-implemented reference state-machine simulations (see strategy_params' help text for each one's EXACT pinned semantics) is used both to CROSS-CHECK expected_result's own declared values before solution_code ever runs, and to grade solution_code's real behavior against. Linear backoff (delay growing by a fixed increment rather than a fixed multiplier) was considered and deliberately left out of this category's initial scope -- it is a real, distinct curve, but noticeably less commonly requested in practice than these four, and this category's own complexity budget (four real semantics plus a bounds-check variant plus a full circuit-breaker state machine) is already the largest of this registry's simulation-style categories; it can be added later as a fifth strategy_type without disturbing any of the other four's own oracle code. write_back-style combined strategies (e.g. circuit-breaker-plus-exponential-backoff-while-closed) are also out of scope -- circuit_breaker here is pure Closed/Open/Half-Open state, with ZERO delay between consecutive CLOSED-state attempts (see its own pinned semantics below); combining it with another strategy's own delay schedule would double this category's oracle surface for a combination real systems do use but this category does not attempt to cover in its first version.

fields.label: Strategy description
fields.help: Natural-language statement of the EXACT strategy solution_code must implement, restating strategy_params' own numbers in prose so a contributor reading only this field (not strategy_params, which is curator-only ground truth never shown as 'the answer' -- see its own help text) knows precisely what to build, e.g. 'fixed delay: wait exactly 2 seconds between attempts, up to 4 attempts total', 'exponential backoff: start at 1 second, double after every failure, cap at 30 seconds, up to 6 attempts total', 'exponential backoff with jitter: same schedule as above but each actual delay must be randomized within +/-25% of that schedule's own value', 'circuit breaker: open the circuit after 3 consecutive failures, wait 10 seconds before trying again (half-open), up to 8 real attempts total'. Must state the SAME numbers as strategy_params -- the two fields are authored together by the curator, describing one strategy from two angles (prose for the contributor to read and implement against; structured JSON for the harness's own oracle to compute against mechanically), the same convention rate_limiting_policy_simulation's policy_description/policy_params pair and caching_strategy's policy_description/policy_params pair already established for this registry.

fields.label: Strategy parameters (curator-authored ground truth, JSON)
fields.help: Curator-authored, fixed context (never graded, never written by the contributor, never sent into solution_code's own Python subprocess at all -- see harness.js's own module doc comment on why the oracle and solution_code run in fully separate address spaces; solution_code is expected to read strategy_description and hardcode its own numbers, exactly like rate_limiting_policy_simulation's RateLimiter/caching_strategy's Cache never receive their own policy_params either). A JSON object whose required keys depend on strategy_type, EVERY strategy_type ALWAYS including max_attempts (a single, uniform meaning across all four: the maximum number of REAL calls to the dependency allowed across the whole row -- a call skipped because a circuit_breaker's circuit is OPEN is never a 'real' call and never counts against this budget): fixed_delay -- {"delay_seconds": N>0, "max_attempts": 2-12}; exponential_backoff -- {"base_delay_seconds": N>0, "multiplier": M, 1<M<=100, "max_delay_seconds": N>=base_delay_seconds, "max_attempts": 2-12}; exponential_backoff_with_jitter -- exponential_backoff's own four keys PLUS {"jitter_ratio": R, 0<R<=1}; circuit_breaker -- {"failure_threshold": F>=1, "reset_timeout_seconds": N>0, "max_attempts": 2-12, with F <= max_attempts-1 (so at least one half-open trial is always reachable after the circuit trips)}. EXACT PINNED SEMANTICS PER strategy_type (author expected_result by hand-applying these EXACT rules): attempt 1 ALWAYS calls the dependency immediately, with zero delay before it, for every strategy_type alike. fixed_delay -- if attempt k (k<max_attempts) fails, wait exactly delay_seconds before attempt k+1; give up with zero further delay the moment attempt max_attempts itself fails. exponential_backoff -- identical attempt/give-up shape; the delay following the n-th consecutive real failure (n counted 1, 2, 3, ... from the start of the row) is min(base_delay_seconds * multiplier^(n-1), max_delay_seconds). exponential_backoff_with_jitter -- identical delay SCHEDULE and identical raw center value raw_n = min(base_delay_seconds * multiplier^(n-1), max_delay_seconds) as exponential_backoff, but the ACTUAL delay solution_code requests must be a genuinely randomized value inside [raw_n*(1-jitter_ratio), raw_n*(1+jitter_ratio)] -- never raw_n itself, repeatedly, with no variation (see solution_code's own help text; the harness bounds-checks real delays rather than exact-matching them for this one strategy_type, since true randomness cannot be exact-matched by design). circuit_breaker -- circuit starts CLOSED with a consecutive-failure counter at 0; while CLOSED, every attempt calls the dependency with ZERO delay from the previous attempt, a real failure increments the counter, and the circuit OPENS the instant the counter reaches failure_threshold (no separate step, same call that trips it is the last real call made while closed); while OPEN, the NEXT attempt in the sequence never calls the dependency at all -- it requests exactly reset_timeout_seconds of delay, transitions to HALF-OPEN, and immediately makes ONE real trial call; a successful trial closes the circuit (and, since it succeeded, ends the whole row in success); a failed trial reopens the circuit immediately (a single half-open failure reopens it -- failure_threshold-many failures are never required a second time) and the open -> (wait reset_timeout_seconds) -> half-open-trial cycle repeats until either a trial succeeds or max_attempts real calls have been made in total. AUTHORING GUIDANCE: prefer clean integer/simple-decimal values (avoid values that only agree exactly under floating-point arithmetic, except where deliberately testing the max_delay_seconds cap) so hand-computed expected values are unambiguous; for circuit_breaker specifically, dependency_behavior/strategy_params must be crafted so the circuit genuinely OPENS at least once (see dependency_behavior's own anti-hardcoding gate) -- a circuit_breaker row whose failure_threshold is never reached tests nothing this strategy_type doesn't already share with plain sequential retrying.

fields.label: Retry/backoff implementation (Python)
fields.help: THE GRADED ARTIFACT. Python code defining EXACTLY ONE top-level function named `retry_call`, with EXACTLY this signature: `def retry_call(dependency, sleep):` -- mirroring how a real retry decorator wraps an arbitrary callable, the harness (never solution_code) owns and constructs BOTH arguments fresh for every row: `dependency` is a zero-argument callable that either returns the dependency's own successful result value or raises an exception, per this row's own harness-scripted dependency_behavior (solution_code must never assume the outcome in advance -- it learns success/failure only by actually calling dependency() and observing whether it returns or raises); `sleep` is a one-argument callable, `sleep(seconds)`, that solution_code MUST call instead of `time.sleep()` for every backoff delay -- the harness intercepts every call, records the exact seconds requested, and returns immediately without ever actually blocking, which is also why a row whose backoff schedule spans simulated minutes still verifies in well under a second of real wall-clock time. retry_call must hardcode THIS row's own strategy_type/strategy_params numbers internally (read from strategy_description; the harness never passes strategy_params in) and implement the matching retry loop: call dependency(); on success, return EXACTLY the value dependency() itself returned (never fabricate/substitute a different success value -- the harness mechanically checks this); on failure, catch the exception, decide (per the declared strategy) whether to sleep() and retry or give up, and if every allowed attempt is exhausted without success, let an exception propagate out of retry_call (any exception type is acceptable -- the harness does not inspect its type or message, only that one genuinely propagated). CRITICAL, MECHANICALLY ENFORCED CONSTRAINT: retry_call must decide every delay using ONLY the strategy it hardcodes internally plus its own attempt bookkeeping -- it must NEVER read the real system clock (no `time.time()`, `time.monotonic()`, `datetime.now()`/`.utcnow()`, or any other real-clock source) and must NEVER really sleep (`time.sleep()` is forbidden outright -- there is no reason to call it at all: the injected `sleep` argument is the ONLY delay mechanism this category ever uses). Enforced two ways, identical to rate_limiting_policy_simulation/caching_strategy's own proven mechanism: (1) a static check rejects solution_code outright if it contains a literal import of time/datetime/calendar or a call to any of their clock-reading functions, or a literal call to `time.sleep()`; (2) as a mechanical backstop against any indirect/dynamic import that dodges (1), the harness replaces sys.modules['time']/['datetime']/['calendar'] with stub objects that raise immediately on ANY attribute access, before solution_code is ever executed. NOTE ON MAX_ATTEMPTS ENFORCEMENT: unlike rate_limiting_policy_simulation/caching_strategy (where the HARNESS itself drives a bounded, externally-counted loop of events/operations), this category's retry loop lives entirely INSIDE solution_code -- there is no external per-call checkpoint the harness can bound the way MAX_EVENTS bounds those two categories. A solution_code that ignores max_attempts and retries forever is instead caught structurally: the harness-scripted dependency_behavior is exactly as long as a CORRECT implementation would ever need, so a buggy implementation that keeps calling dependency() past that point keeps receiving simulated failures forever, and either eventually raises (caught as a real call-count mismatch against expected_result) or spins until this row's own execution timeout fires -- treated as a real failure, not an infra problem, identical to this registry's established 'a genuine timeout on tiny, fast work is itself meaningful signal' convention for a pathological/adversarial busy loop.

fields.label: Simulated dependency call script
fields.help: JSON array of 2-12 entries, each exactly the string "fail" or "succeed" -- the ordered outcome of every REAL call solution_code's retry_call makes to the harness-injected dependency() callable (a call skipped because a circuit_breaker's circuit is OPEN never consumes an entry here at all -- see strategy_params' own pinned semantics). This is the harness-controlled SCRIPT driving the simulated dependency; solution_code never sees it directly, only the dependency() callable itself, which raises on "fail" and returns a fixed (harness-generated, per-row-unique, structurally unguessable) success marker value on "succeed". The harness's own independent oracle (see harness.js's own module doc comment) computes, from strategy_type + strategy_params ALONE, the EXACT number of real calls a correct implementation would ever make before reaching a definitive outcome (success, or exhausting max_attempts) -- dependency_behavior's own length must equal that number EXACTLY: too short and even a correct solution_code would run out of scripted entries before finishing; too long and the trailing entries could never be reached by any correct implementation, an unambiguous dataset-authoring defect either way, rejected before solution_code is ever run. ANTI-HARDCODING, MECHANICALLY ENFORCED: (1) at least 2 entries are required for every strategy_type (a length-1 script can never exercise a genuine RETRY at all -- the very first call already decides everything); (2) for strategy_type "circuit_breaker" specifically, the sequence must cause the circuit to genuinely OPEN at least once (per strategy_params' own failure_threshold) -- a circuit_breaker row that never actually trips the circuit tests nothing this strategy_type doesn't already share with plain sequential retrying, and is rejected outright. AUTHORING GUIDANCE: an all-"fail" script (ending in expected_result.outcome "exhausted") is a legitimate, valuable row -- it is the ONLY way to exercise the 'give up' path and, for circuit_breaker, the open-circuit/half-open-retry path; author some rows this way, not only ones that eventually succeed.

fields.label: Expected result (curator-computed ground truth, JSON)
fields.help: JSON object `{"outcome": "success" | "exhausted", "final_attempts": N, "delay_sequence": [...]}, hand-computed by the curator via strategy_params/dependency_behavior's own EXACT pinned semantics (see strategy_params' help text), then independently double-checked by the harness's own reference-oracle computation before solution_code ever runs -- a declared expected_result that is self-consistent-looking but does not actually match what strategy_type/strategy_params/dependency_behavior together produce is rejected as a dataset-authoring defect, not silently accepted (identical discipline to rate_limiting_policy_simulation's timeline.expected / caching_strategy's operations[].expected_*). `outcome` is "success" if dependency_behavior's own script lets a real call eventually succeed within max_attempts, else "exhausted". `final_attempts` is the exact total count of REAL dependency() calls a correct implementation makes before reaching that outcome (always equal to dependency_behavior's own array length -- see that field's own help text for why). `delay_sequence` is the exact, ORDERED list of every delay value a correct implementation requests via sleep() -- for fixed_delay/exponential_backoff/circuit_breaker this is compared to solution_code's own real sleep() calls via EXACT numeric equality (a tiny floating-point tolerance only); for exponential_backoff_with_jitter, delay_sequence must instead hold the RAW, pre-jitter center values (exactly as exponential_backoff itself would compute them -- the harness cross-checks THESE exactly against its own oracle) and solution_code's own real, randomized sleep() calls are then checked only for falling within +/-jitter_ratio of each already-verified center value, never for exact equality (see harness.js's own module doc comment on why exact-matching genuine randomness is infeasible by design).
